articles.title: Gestante entra em trabalho de parto e filho nasce no carro em Campos | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipe do Hospital São José prestou atendimento emergencial à mãe e ao recém-nascido, que foram transferidos em seguida para o Hospital Plantadores de Cana.
articles.summary: Equipe do Hospital São José prestou atendimento emergencial à mãe e ao recém-nascido, que foram transferidos em seguida para o Hospital Plantadores de Cana.
articles.body:
Uma gestante deu à luz dentro de um carro de aplicativo enquanto estava a caminho da maternidade, em Campos dos Goytacazes , no Norte Fluminense.

Era pouco antes das 8h de quinta-feira (15) quando o motorista resolveu mudar o caminho e parou na porta do Hospital São José, pedindo ajuda. O primeiro funcionário chegou já pegando o bebê no colo.

Médicos e enfermeiros correram para ajudar a retirar a placenta e levaram a mãe e o bebê de ambulância para o Hospital Plantadores de Cana (HPC), referência em atendimento obstétrico. Os dois passam bem.

A enfermeira Marcela Gomes contou que, assim que viram que o bebê já havia nascido, se apressaram em pegar os instrumentos e realizar os procedimentos finais ali mesmo no carro.

"Quando chegamos, foi uma surpresa, porque o bebê já tinha nascido. Corremos para chamar a médica, ela cortou o cordão umbilical e esperamos o tempo adequado e seguro para a retirada da placenta. A técnica de enfermagem buscou a bandeja, montamos o campo esterilizado e preparamos o bebê para ser transferido para a maternidade", relatou a enfermeira.

A médica Sthephany Mozzer destacou que o atendimento de emergência foi conduzido de acordo com os protocolos de segurança hospitalar, com a utilização dos materiais adequados para os cuidados com a mãe e o bebê.

"A mãe iria para o HPC, mas não deu tempo, pois já estava em período expulsivo. O bebê chorou, veio com saúde. Foi tudo muito rápido. Era o quinto filho dela por parto normal", contou.

Após a conclusão dos procedimentos, a mãe e o recém-nascido foram transferidos para o Hospital Plantadores de Cana (HPC) — Foto: Hospital São José

articles.title: Amigos se despedem do colunista Marcos Raffou em Aracaju | G1
articles.standfirst: Raffou movimentou a cena cultural e social do estado com a idealização de bailes e do prêmio ‘Gente Gentíssima’, troféu que reconhecia personalidades, empresas e profissionais da imprensa.
articles.summary: Raffou movimentou a cena cultural e social do estado com a idealização de bailes e do prêmio ‘Gente Gentíssima’, troféu que reconhecia personalidades, empresas e profissionais da imprensa.
articles.body:
Amigos se despedem do colunista Marcos Raffou em Aracaju. — Foto: Anderson Barbosa/ TV Sergipe

Amigos e familiares se despedem do colunista social Marcos Antônio Fernandes, conhecido como Marcos Raffou, nesta sexta-feira (16), em Aracaju . Ele tinha 67 anos e estava internado no Hospital de Urgências de Sergipe (Huse), onde tratava um câncer.

O velório acontece na funerária Osaf, no Centro de Aracaju e o sepultamento está marcado para as 16h, no Cemitério Santa Isabel.

Natural de São Paulo, ele se estabeleceu em Sergipe e atuou inicialmente como cabeleireiro de artistas e autoridades.

Posteriormente, como colunista social, organizou bailes da cena cultural do estado e idealizou o prêmio ‘Gente Gentíssima’, troféu que homenageava personalidades, empresas e profissionais da imprensa.

articles.title: Desabamento em Niterói: duas pessoas são resgatadas em estado grave | G1
articles.standfirst: Mulher e adolescente foram levados para o Hospital Estadual Azevedo Lima. Defesa Civil foi acionada para avaliar a estrutura.
articles.summary: Vítimas de desabamento em Niterói foram levadas ao Hospital Azevedo Lima após resgate do Corpo de Bombeiros no bairro do Caramujo nesta sexta-feira.
articles.body:
Imóvel desaba em Niterói — Foto: Divulgação/CBMERJ

Uma mulher adulta e um adolescente foram retirados em estado grave dos escombros de uma edificação que desabou na manhã desta sexta-feira (16), no Caramujo, em Niterói .

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, os militares foram acionados para a Rua da Horta, e equipes do Quartel de Niterói (3º GBM) foram mobilizadas por volta das 7h.

As vítimas foram encaminhadas ao Hospital Estadual Azevedo Lima. Os nomes não foram divulgados.

A Defesa Civil de Niterói foi acionada para avaliar as questões estruturais.

articles.title: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall
articles.summary: Joshua Foster "lost control" of his son while showing him the view of a water park from a window.
articles.body:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him , Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.

Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.

The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.

"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.

His failure to establish that the window was closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.

"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences."

The judge said there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.

She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".

In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".

While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.

After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".

He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.

"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.

He described his client as an "incredible father".

"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

articles.title: Pope Leo's lung tumor raises questions about cancer risk for nonsmokers
articles.summary: An oncologist says Pope Leo XIV has a roughly 90% chance of cure if the lung cancer is stage 1, but pathology results will determine next steps.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after a scheduled surgery, the Vatican announced Tuesday. After undergoing thoracic surgery, where surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. The diagnosis had been suspected based on testing conducted before the procedure, according to the Holy See Press Office. POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS The pope reportedly does not smoke and does not have a known history of smoking. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicates that most lung cancer deaths (80%) are caused by smoking. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, representing about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. It is also the most common type among non-smokers. NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER In an interview with Fox News Digital, Lary Robinson, M.D., an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the pope’s health status, as the lung nodule was "felt to be malignant." About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers — including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients. "But [the pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a stage 1 cancer," the doctor added. If the pope’s cancer is stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90%, depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread. HEALTHY DIETS SPARK LUNG CANCER RISK IN NON-SMOKERS AS PESTICIDES LOOM "We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he had a stage 1 cancer and whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said. "Size matters in lung nodules and lung cancer – the larger the cancer, the worse outlook it is, because it's more likely to be advanced and have spread." Risk factors for never-smokers Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking. Other factors like family history and genetic predisposition can play a role, experts say. Recent research discovered that a rare genetic mutation in the gene EGFR T790M increased lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to findings published in the journal Science. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who were not carriers. Robinson added that other types of smoking, like pipes and cigars, can increase the risk of lung cancer, as well as heavy use of marijuana. Another risk factor is exposure to environmental toxins, such as diesel exhaust and radon, according to the oncologist. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Unfortunately, probably over half of the people who are never-smokers with lung cancer come into stage 4 disease," Robinson said. "And that's higher than people who are smokers or former smokers, so they start out at a worse stage in general." Symptoms and screening In most cases, early-stage lung cancer will not come with any symptoms, according to Robinson. In those who do have symptoms, however, the most common are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Unexplained weight loss can result from any form of cancer, the oncologist noted. Neurological symptoms, like persistent headaches, may also warrant seeing a doctor. Lung cancer is rare in younger adults, which is why annual CT screening is generally recommended starting at age 50 for those at high risk, the doctor said. People considered at high risk include current smokers with at least a 20 pack-year history, as well as former smokers who quit within the past 15 years. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Only about 15% of the people who are eligible get screened, unfortunately," Robinson said. "I'm hoping that within four or five years, a screening CT scan will only be confirmatory after they have a positive blood test done at your doctor's office." That approach could make screening easier and potentially help detect more lung cancers, according to the doctor.

articles.title: This Is the No. 1 Risk Factor for Dementia That You Can Actually Prevent, According to a Geriatrician
articles.summary: As we get older, the world gradually starts looking and sounding a little different.
articles.body: As we get older, the world gradually starts looking and sounding a little different. Our vision may not be as sharp as it once was, and we may need to hit the “increase volume” button on the remote a few extra times to hear the television. Most people will experience some degree of age-related hearing loss, which usually becomes more apparent over the age of 60, Dr. Stephanie Rogers, a professor of medicine in the division of geriatrics at the University of California San Francisco School of Medicine, tells TODAY.com. However, hearing problems can begin even earlier in life. And leaving them unaddressed may seriously impact the brain, increasing the risk of cognitive decline, says Rogers. Longevity Tip of the Day: Address Hearing Loss to Lower Your Risk of Developing Dementia Untreated hearing loss is the No. 1 modifiable risk factor for dementia, says Rogers. Modifiable risk factors are behaviors or exposures that can influence our risk of developing a disease. Unlike non-modifiable risk factors, such as our genetics, these can be changed. Hearing loss typically begins subtly in early adulthood and slowly accrues over decades. “Loud noise damage can start to occur in your teens and 20s,” says Rogers. If you experience noticeable hearing changes or problems during mid-life, it’s time to get checked out. People who develop hearing loss between the ages of 40-65 may have a greater risk for developing dementia, according to the Alzheimer’s Society. Dementia refers to a group of symptoms that affect memory, speech and social abilities. It affects at least 7 million Americans. Why It Matters Hearing loss can increase the risk of dementia in a few different ways, Rogers says. First, it puts a huge cognitive load on the brain. “When one can’t hear as well, the brain expends a lot of energy trying to decode speech. This depletes the reserve available for other cognitive tasks, like the encoding of memories or memory consolidation,” says Rogers. The reduced auditory input may also cause certain parts of the brain to atrophy or weaken because they aren’t being used as much anymore, says Rogers. Sensory deprivation can also reduce neuroplasticity, or our brain’s ability to adapt and rewire itself. Finally, hearing loss can contribute to social isolation, which is another major risk factor for dementia. “Many people who can’t hear as well start to not participate in conversations or social situations,” says Rogers. It can cause an otherwise outgoing, bubbly person to become more withdrawn. Fortunately, hearing loss can be addressed to help reduce the risk of dementia, Rogers says. How To Get Started First, it’s important to recognize the symptoms of hearing loss. “Usually the first sign is difficulty understanding speech when there is background noise, i.e. in a restaurant,” says Rogers. Sounds may become muffled, you may find yourself asking people to repeat themselves, or needing to turn the radio or television volume higher, per the Mayo Clinic. If you’re experiencing any of these issues, talk to your doctor. They may refer you to a specialist for further testing. “I use the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck surgery guidelines for hearing loss screening,” says Rogers. “Everyone should get screening, whether you notice hearing loss or not, at age 50, then every three to five years until age 65, then every one to three years after age 65,” Rogers adds. Hearing aids are a first-line treatment for age-related hearing loss. “There are over-the-counter versions for patients with mild-to-moderate loss, which can help the majority of people. There are also prescription hearing aids for more severe hearing loss,” Rogers adds. In addition to addressing hearing loss, Rogers recommends other lifestyle habits to promote brain and heart health, which may reduce dementia risk. “Things like controlling cholesterol, blood sugar, blood pressure ... not smoking and avoiding excessive alcohol intake, and consistent exercise are also important.” TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: ‘Dowry murder’: Woman’s body cremated at in-laws’ doorstep
articles.summary: Muzaffarpur: 19-year-old married woman found dead; family alleges dowry murder, names husband and in-laws. Body cremated at in-laws’ doorstep; probe on.
articles.body: Patna: A newly married woman was found dead at her house in Rajwara Dih village under Mushahari police station area in Muzaffarpur district on Wednesday night, following which her family alleged murder. Her relatives later cremated the body of Gunja Kumari, 19, at her in-laws’ doorstep on Thursday evening.Gunja’s family has accused four people, including her husband Kundan Kumar, of murdering her over dowry. Kundan, his brother Chandan Paswan and other in-laws are absconding. Police have registered a case based on the family’s application and started an investigation.Gunja’s maternal uncle Chhotu Kumar said a ward member of Rajwara village informed him about her death. Her family reached Rajwara Dih from Kanti around midnight on Wednesday and found the body lying in a room with marks on her neck. Police reached the spot, pacified the family and sent the body to SKMCH for post-mortem.Chhotu said Gunja and Kundan met during the Rudra Mahayagya in Simraha Chaturbhuj village near Jhapahan in 2024. They fell in love, eloped and married. The families later agreed to their marriage, following which they were married again according to Hindu rituals.Gunja’s grandmother Siya Janki Devi alleged Kundan had been torturing her for dowry since their marriage. She said the family was preparing to give dowry items on Dhanteras, but Gunja died before that.According to Chhotu, Gunja had returned to her maternal home around three months ago and was brought back after a panchayat decision.In the FIR, the family has accused Kundan, Chandan, Priyanka Devi and Sulekha Devi of murder.Mushahari SHO Subodh Kumar Mehta said, “After the death of the married woman, police had reached the spot on information of ruckus. People were pacified and the body was sent for post-mortem.”Mehta said police later learned about the cremation at the in-laws’ doorstep. “Action will be taken in this matter also. articles.title: Trump administration advances plan for peptide drugs favored by RFK Jr.
articles.summary: Health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow compounding pharmacies to make certain peptides including BPC-157.
articles.body: U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow specialty pharmacies to produce certain peptides, a class of largely unregulated injections that have become popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers. Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services submitted a peptides “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a posting Thursday on a government website. The plan was sent to the Office of Management and Budget, which reviews federal rules and regulations with the potential for significant economic impact. HHS officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon. Peptides are the building blocks of more complex proteins, triggering hormones inside the body needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss. But the ones at issue here haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. Nevertheless, they have gained a foothold among Americans interested in bulking up, looking younger or boosting energy. Those uses are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration and most of the data on peptides comes from animal studies. Before joining the administration, Kennedy publicly declared that “FDA’s war” on peptides and other wellness products would soon end. After becoming health secretary, Kennedy said U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans were increasingly turning to “gray market” peptides made in China and other countries. Those products remain widely available for purchase via online platforms like TikTok. The White House filing doesn’t give specifics of the new policy, but two people familiar with the plan say it is intended to allow pharmacies to temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, a chemical promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. The update is the latest indication that Kennedy and other Trump administration officials are looking to ease access to unproven products that are popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Some of the biggest MAHA figures sell peptide injections and supplements. The FDA previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances that are too risky to be compounded by pharmacies. Possible risks include contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth, according to the FDA. But earlier this year, Kennedy directed the agency to reconsider a short list of chemicals that have been widely promoted by wellness influencers and fitness celebrities. In July, a panel of external FDA advisers recommended the agency drop its restrictions on six of the seven peptides put before them. That recommendation went against the scientific conclusion of FDA’s staff scientists, who reiterated that none of the peptides had been studied enough to establish their safety and effectiveness. The new policy sent to the White House would essentially assure compounding pharmacies — specialty businesses that mix customized medications that aren’t available from traditional drugmakers — that they won’t be targeted for producing certain peptides, according to the people familiar with the plan. That approach, known as enforcement discretion, allows the FDA to selectively choose to not enforce some of its own regulations. Formally adding the peptides to FDA’s list of drugs that are safe for compounding would require federal rulemaking, a process that could take years and involves multiple rounds of public comment. It was not immediately clear if the administration still plans to pursue that process. The proposal was quickly praised online by some Kennedy allies who sell peptides. “This is huge,” Brigham Buhler, a wellness clinic operator who sells peptides through an online service, posted on X. “This isn’t about whether you’re for or against peptides. It’s about whether you’re for or against MEDICAL FREEDOM.” The panel of outside experts that met in July was selected by Kennedy’s health department and included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field. The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers and Noom. Both companies recently announced plans to offer peptides to their customers if the federal government eases access. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth $2 billion to $3 billion.

articles.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.

Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.

Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next

On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.

His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".

The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

articles.title: I lost half my right lung to cancer. Pope Leo's diagnosis gives me hope
articles.summary: A lung cancer survivor compares her stage 1B diagnosis and surgery to Pope Leo's adenocarcinoma, urging expanded screening beyond heavy smokers.
articles.body: When Pope Leo told the crowd in St. Peter's Square on Sunday that doctors had found "a small, localized nodule" in his lung, the reassurances came fast. Most nodules are benign, media medical experts quickly said. Probably nothing to worry about. I heard the same reassurances about my own lung not long ago. They were wrong then, and on Tuesday the Vatican confirmed they were wrong now. The nodule was adenocarcinoma, lung cancer. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Holy Father's right lung through a few small incisions, guided by a camera rather than an open chest, and he was back in his room the same afternoon. POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS That is almost exactly what happened to me. Half of my right lung was removed just 12 months ago, and I was running just four weeks after that. So, my first reaction when I heard the pope's diagnosis was not dread. It was hope. I was 43, a mother of four, a daily runner, and the daughter of a lung doctor. The morning I learned I had lung cancer, I had already completed a six-mile run without a hint that anything was wrong. I had no symptoms. Under current guidelines, I was not supposed to be at risk, and I did not qualify for screening. POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS My diagnosis came from a scan I chose, not from a symptom. My husband and I have always leaned toward proactive testing, and at his urging I scheduled what I assumed would be a baseline full-body scan, paid for out of pocket. It showed a 3.8-centimeter nodule on my right lung. Initial advice from the reading radiologist recommended to follow-up if symptoms occurred. But with a father as a lung doctor and a friend as a lung radiologist, they pushed me to follow up sooner. The new low dose CT of my chest showed the mass had grown in just two months. But that scan led to a diagnosis of stage 1B lung cancer and, like the pope, to surgery to remove it. Still, no symptoms ever appeared. Four weeks to the day after my operation, I was on a plane. I was running again within weeks. Caught early and handled by a skilled medical team and a surgeon who does this every day, lung cancer is not a death sentence. It is a survivable disease, a fixable problem. If the pope keeps his November trip to South America, he will board that plane about as far out from surgery as I was. DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH So the gloom I see in my text threads with Catholic friends this week is misplaced. What should worry Americans is something else entirely. The pope's cancer was found during a routine checkup. Mine was found because I paid for a scan no one recommended. Most Americans get neither. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States and one of the most expensive cancers to treat, because it is usually found late. Current guidelines recommend screening only for adults ages 50 to 80 with a heavy smoking history. Fewer than one in five people who qualify ever get the scan. And nearly two-thirds of people diagnosed with lung cancer would not have qualified at all. I am one of them. POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS Stage at diagnosis is the strongest predictor of both survival and cost. Found at stage I, five-year survival can exceed 90%. Yet most cases are still found after the disease has spread, when curative treatment becomes unlikely. There is a fix on the table. The Saving Health by Identifying Risk for Americans (SHIRA) Act, a draft bill now circulating in the White House, HHS and Congress, would make lung cancer screening free to the patient under Medicare — no copay, no deductible. It would cover veterans exposed to burn pits, guarantee a first scan to cancer survivors and those with a family history, and require Medicare to modernize who counts as "high risk" so that never-smokers, like me, stop being invisible. It builds a path toward age-based screening after 40, the way we already screen for breast and colorectal cancer. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I was fortunate. A preventive scan, a persistent friend and father, and an early diagnosis gave me a future I might not otherwise have had. The pope was fortunate too: a routine check found his cancer before he felt a thing. Luck should not decide who survives lung cancer. Screening policy should. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP I am praying for the pope this week, and I am confident. I would like every American to have the same reason for confidence he does.

articles.title: Ivy-League educated pediatrician allegedly murdered by husband who then set home on fire: police
articles.summary: Julia Pederson, a Stanford-educated pediatrician at UPMC, was allegedly strangled by husband Jonathan Gatto before he set their Harrisburg home ablaze.
articles.body: A highly-regarded pediatrician, mother and wife was murdered by her husband, investigators say. Julia Pederson, 41, of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was killed after police say her husband, Jonathan Gatto, 41, strangled her inside the family's home and intentionally set it on fire. Authorities said the fire happened on Saturday, Oct. 10. Four days later, Gatto was arrested and charged with murder and arson, among other charges. TEXAS DAD FACES MURDER CHARGE AFTER ESTRANGED WIFE FOUND DEAD AT SUBURBAN HOME: POLICE The Harrisburg Bureau of Police said, "The investigation ultimately revealed that the death of the victim, a 41-year-old female, was not caused by a fire." Reports say the couple's 7-year-old daughter was also sleeping in an upstairs bedroom at the time of the incident, according to KATV.
